texts.orig: To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.

texts.orig: Go's [`net/http`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http) package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:
texts.text: Go's [`net/http`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http) package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: **TCP handshake (1 RTT)** : the client sends a `SYN` packet, the server replies with `SYN-ACK` , and the client replies with `ACK` . Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final `ACK` , establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).
texts.text: **TCP handshake (1 RTT)** : the client sends a `SYN` packet, the server replies with `SYN-ACK` , and the client replies with `ACK` . Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final `ACK` , establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: **TLS handshake (2 RTT)** : next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server's identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.
texts.text: **TLS handshake (2 RTT)** : next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server's identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: **HTTP request** : with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.
texts.text: **HTTP request** : with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.

This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Connection reuse
texts.text: Connection reuse

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:
texts.text: To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: **HTTP/1.0** : while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a `Connection: keep-alive` header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a `Connection: close` header.
texts.text: **HTTP/1.0** : while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a `Connection: keep-alive` header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a `Connection: close` header.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: **HTTP/1.1** : connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a `Connection: close` header.
texts.text: **HTTP/1.1** : connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a `Connection: close` header.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: **HTTP/2** : multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.
texts.text: **HTTP/2** : multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: When connection reuse fails
texts.text: When connection reuse fails

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two `GET` requests are sent to [index.golang.org](https://index.golang.org/) over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:
texts.text: In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two `GET` requests are sent to [index.golang.org](https://index.golang.org/) over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As shown in the diagram, [`net/http.Get`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Get) reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate [`net/http.Response`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Response) , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from [`net/http.Response.Body`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Response.Body) .
texts.text: As shown in the diagram, [`net/http.Get`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Get) reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate [`net/http.Response`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Response) , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from [`net/http.Response.Body`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Response.Body) .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, [`net/http`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http) can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` header).

texts.orig: Through Go 1.26, when `resp.Body.Close` is called, [`net/http`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http) sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Where failed connection reuse hurts
texts.text: Where failed connection reuse hurts

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.
texts.text: This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response's status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as `{"success": true, "message": "update processed"}` . This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.
texts.text: As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response's status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as `{"success": true, "message": "update processed"}` . This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, [`encoding/json.Decoder`](https://go.dev/pkg/encoding/json#Decoder) stops reading as soon as it sees the closing `}` of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

texts.orig: The current state and conclusion
texts.text: The current state and conclusion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Starting in Go 1.27, [`net/http.Transport`](https://go.dev/pkg/net/http#Transport) automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the `Connection: close` header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since Go 1.26, we have supported an experimental `amd64` SIMD API. Now in Go 1.27, we support two more architectures: `arm64` and `wasm` .
texts.text: Since Go 1.26, we have supported an experimental `amd64` SIMD API. Now in Go 1.27, we support two more architectures: `arm64` and `wasm` .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The new APIs can be accessed by setting `GOEXPERIMENT=simd` when building a program. They are defined in the `simd/archsimd` package.
texts.text: The new APIs can be accessed by setting `GOEXPERIMENT=simd` when building a program. They are defined in the `simd/archsimd` package.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: `archsimd` is the lower-level infrastructure that `simd` builds on, essentially the intrinsics layer in other languages. For exotic operations that only exist on a specific architecture, users can access them by transitioning from `simd` to `archsimd` (via `ToArch` and `<Types>FromArch` ). For details, please refer to the [simd blog](https://go.dev/blog/simd-experiment) post.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: What is SIMD
texts.text: What is SIMD

texts.label: text
texts.orig: SIMD stands for Single Instruction, Multiple Data. SIMD instructions operate on wide registers (128-bit, 256-bit, or more) containing multiple 8- to 64-bit elements, performing operations across all elements in parallel. Wider registers and parallel execution provide a significant performance boost to algorithms that can take advantage of them.
texts.text: SIMD stands for Single Instruction, Multiple Data. SIMD instructions operate on wide registers (128-bit, 256-bit, or more) containing multiple 8- to 64-bit elements, performing operations across all elements in parallel. Wider registers and parallel execution provide a significant performance boost to algorithms that can take advantage of them.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Until now, anyone who wanted to use SIMD in Go had to endure the friction of writing assembly language. The new `archsimd` package is here to change that.
texts.text: Until now, anyone who wanted to use SIMD in Go had to endure the friction of writing assembly language. The new `archsimd` package is here to change that.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Goals
texts.text: Goals

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The goal is to support as many SIMD instructions across different architectures as possible. Currently, we have `amd64` , `arm64` , and `wasm` available. Our `amd64` support has the largest API surface, covering AVX, AVX2, and many AVX-512 extensions. Our `arm64` support currently covers NEON, with SVE and some SVE2 already on the way. Our `wasm` support is also mostly complete, thanks to its well-defined 128-bit SIMD abstraction.
texts.text: The goal is to support as many SIMD instructions across different architectures as possible. Currently, we have `amd64` , `arm64` , and `wasm` available. Our `amd64` support has the largest API surface, covering AVX, AVX2, and many AVX-512 extensions. Our `arm64` support currently covers NEON, with SVE and some SVE2 already on the way. Our `wasm` support is also mostly complete, thanks to its well-defined 128-bit SIMD abstraction.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Some users might be interested in matrix extensions on certain architectures, such as AMX and SME. We haven't fully settled on how to represent matrices effectively in Go, so they are not yet supported, but we might support them in the future.

texts.orig: Types
texts.text: Types

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The architecture-specific SIMD API is imported from `simd/archsimd` . `archsimd` uses distinct struct types, such as `Float32x4` , `Int32x8` , or `Uint8x16` , to signal the shape and element type of each vector, and defines operations as methods on those types. At this moment, `archsimd` supports only fixed-width vector extensions. Scalable vector extensions like `arm64` SVE and RVV will have different struct types to represent vectors. Mask types also come with vector-like shapes, e.g., `Mask32x4` .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Across different vector widths, element types, and architectures, we use the same method name whenever operations are semantically identical:
texts.text: Across different vector widths, element types, and architectures, we use the same method name whenever operations are semantically identical:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Regardless of vector width or architecture, element-wise addition is simply `x.Add(y)` ; the type of `x` determines which instruction to emit. Instead of 18 different function names for addition, there is only one method name.
texts.text: Regardless of vector width or architecture, element-wise addition is simply `x.Add(y)` ; the type of `x` determines which instruction to emit. Instead of 18 different function names for addition, there is only one method name.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: When instructions on different architectures look similar at a glance but differ in edge-case behavior, we give them distinct names so differences don't silently bite you. For example, 16-byte table lookup on `amd64` ( `VPSHUFB` ) zeros the output byte when the index is negative ( `index < 0` ) and wraps modulo 16 otherwise, so we call it `PermuteOrZero` . On `arm64` NEON ( `VTBL` ) and `wasm` ( `i8x16.swizzle` ), any out-of-range index ( `index < 0 || index >= 16` ) zeros the output byte, so we call it `LookupOrZero` .

texts.orig: Another example is matrix transpose. On `amd64` , the permutation instructions are shaped in a non-portable way, so using `simd` is cumbersome and might incur emulations. func Transpose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7 archsimd.Int32x8) (
    b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 archsimd.Int32x8) {
    if !archsimd.X86.AVX2() {
        // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted.
        return slowTranspose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7)
    }
    /*
            LOW  HIGH
        a0: abcd efgh
        a1: ijkl mnop
        a2: qrst uvwx
        a3: 0123 4567
        a4: ABCD EFGH
        a5: IJKL MNOP
        a6: QRST UVWX
        a7: 89yz YZ$@
    */
    t0 := a0.InterleaveLoGrouped(a1) // t0 = aibj emfn
    t1 := a0.InterleaveHiGrouped(a1) // t1 = ckdl gohp
    t2 := a2.InterleaveLoGrouped(a3) // t2 = q0r1 u4v5
    t3 := a2.InterleaveHiGrouped(a3) // t3 = s2t3 w6x7
    t4 := a4.InterleaveLoGrouped(a5) // t4 = AIBJ EMFN
    t5 := a4.InterleaveHiGrouped(a5) // t5 = CKDL GOHP
    t6 := a6.InterleaveLoGrouped(a7) // t6 = Q8R9 UYVZ
    t7 := a6.InterleaveHiGrouped(a7) // t7 = SyTz W$X@

    a0 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t2) // a0 = aiq0 emu4
    a1 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t2) // a1 = bjr1 fnv5
    a2 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t3) // a2 = cks2 gow6
    a3 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t3) // a3 = dlt3 hpx7
    a4 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t6) // a4 = AIQ8 EMUY
    a5 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t6) // a5 = BJR9 FNVZ
    a6 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t7) // a6 = CKSy GOW$
    a7 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t7) // a7 = DLTz HPX@

    b0 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a4) // b0 = aiq0 AIQ8
    b1 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a5) // b1 = bjr1 BJR9
    b2 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a6) // b2 = cks2 CKSy
    b3 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a7) // b3 = dlt3 DLTz
    b4 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a4) // b4 = emu4 EMUY
    b5 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a5) // b5 = fnv5 FNVZ
    b6 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a6) // b6 = gow6 GOW$
    b7 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a7) // b7 = hpx7 HPX@

    return
}

func Transpose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7 archsimd.Int32x8) (
    b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 archsimd.Int32x8) {
    if !archsimd.X86.AVX2() {
        // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted.
        return slowTranspose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7)
    }
    /*
            LOW  HIGH
        a0: abcd efgh
        a1: ijkl mnop
        a2: qrst uvwx
        a3: 0123 4567
        a4: ABCD EFGH
        a5: IJKL MNOP
        a6: QRST UVWX
        a7: 89yz YZ$@
    */
    t0 := a0.InterleaveLoGrouped(a1) // t0 = aibj emfn
    t1 := a0.InterleaveHiGrouped(a1) // t1 = ckdl gohp
    t2 := a2.InterleaveLoGrouped(a3) // t2 = q0r1 u4v5
    t3 := a2.InterleaveHiGrouped(a3) // t3 = s2t3 w6x7
    t4 := a4.InterleaveLoGrouped(a5) // t4 = AIBJ EMFN
    t5 := a4.InterleaveHiGrouped(a5) // t5 = CKDL GOHP
    t6 := a6.InterleaveLoGrouped(a7) // t6 = Q8R9 UYVZ
    t7 := a6.InterleaveHiGrouped(a7) // t7 = SyTz W$X@

    a0 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t2) // a0 = aiq0 emu4
    a1 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t2) // a1 = bjr1 fnv5
    a2 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t3) // a2 = cks2 gow6
    a3 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t3) // a3 = dlt3 hpx7
    a4 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t6) // a4 = AIQ8 EMUY
    a5 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t6) // a5 = BJR9 FNVZ
    a6 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t7) // a6 = CKSy GOW$
    a7 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t7) // a7 = DLTz HPX@

    b0 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a4) // b0 = aiq0 AIQ8
    b1 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a5) // b1 = bjr1 BJR9
    b2 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a6) // b2 = cks2 CKSy
    b3 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a7) // b3 = dlt3 DLTz
    b4 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a4) // b4 = emu4 EMUY
    b5 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a5) // b5 = fnv5 FNVZ
    b6 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a6) // b6 = gow6 GOW$
    b7 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a7) // b7 = hpx7 HPX@

    return
}

texts.orig: At first glance these choices might look like minor stylistic preferences, but each of them is chosen for an important performance or correctness reason:
texts.text: At first glance these choices might look like minor stylistic preferences, but each of them is chosen for an important performance or correctness reason:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: CPU feature checks ( `archsimd.X86.*` , `archsimd.ARM64.*` ) On `amd64` , we provide runtime feature checks like `archsimd.X86.AVX()` , `AVX2()` , `AVX512()` , and extension checks like `AVX512GFNI()` or `AVX512VNNI()` ; on `arm64` , NEON is always available, and we provide checks for optional extensions like `archsimd.ARM64.PMULL()` , `SVE()` , and `SVE2()` . The compiler doesn't know ahead of time whether the machine running your binary supports optional SIMD extensions. If you don't guard your SIMD code with the appropriate feature check, your program may crash with `SIGILL` on hardware that lacks the instruction. Just as importantly, CPU feature checks act as **compiler optimization hints** . For example, AVX-512 supports hardware merge-masking on instruction outputs. How the compiler lowers `x.Add(y).IfElse(m, z)` on a 128-bit or 256-bit vector depends on which CPU features are known to be available. If the code is not guarded by `archsimd.X86.AVX512()` , the compiler must conservatively emit a vector `VPADD` followed by a `VPBLEND` instruction. Inside an `if archsimd.X86.AVX512()` block, however, the compiler knows AVX-512 is available and fuses the sequence into a single merge-masked AVX-512 `VPADD` instruction.

Just as importantly, CPU feature checks act as **compiler optimization hints** . For example, AVX-512 supports hardware merge-masking on instruction outputs. How the compiler lowers `x.Add(y).IfElse(m, z)` on a 128-bit or 256-bit vector depends on which CPU features are known to be available. If the code is not guarded by `archsimd.X86.AVX512()` , the compiler must conservatively emit a vector `VPADD` followed by a `VPBLEND` instruction. Inside an `if archsimd.X86.AVX512()` block, however, the compiler knows AVX-512 is available and fuses the sequence into a single merge-masked AVX-512 `VPADD` instruction.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Bounds check elimination in strided loops How you write the loop bound determines whether the compiler's `prove` pass can eliminate slice bounds checks inside the loop. In `i + v.Len() <= len(src)` , the addition `i + v.Len()` could theoretically overflow to a negative `int` if `len(src)` were near `math.MaxInt` , which prevents the compiler from proving that `i` is always non-negative and in-bounds. Writing `i < len(src)-v.Len()+1` avoids that potential overflow, allowing the loop body to compile with zero bounds checks.

Writing `i < len(src)-v.Len()+1` avoids that potential overflow, allowing the loop body to compile with zero bounds checks.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Keeping vectors in registers (avoiding large composite types) `Transpose8` passes 8 vector parameters rather than a struct of 8 fields or an `[8]archsimd.Int32x8` array because Go's ABI and SSA backend currently place large composite types in memory rather than in registers (a known issue tracked at [#24416](https://go.dev/issue/24416) ). Because SIMD vectors are 16 to 64 bytes each, spilling them to the stack hurts performance much more than spilling scalar values. This applies to both function parameters and local variables, so avoid wrapping SIMD vectors inside large arrays or structs in hot loops. There are ongoing efforts to promote composite memory accesses back into registers, which have not yet landed in Go 1.27.

texts.orig: For Go 1.28 and beyond, we are actively working on completing `arm64` SVE and SVE2 support in `archsimd` (introducing width-agnostic scalable vector types like `archsimd.Float32s` backed directly by hardware SVE registers and predicates) and wiring it into `simd` . We also plan to expand `archsimd` to additional architectures such as `riscv64` , `ppc64` , `s390x` , and `loong64` , improve register promotion for composite types, and continue filling in instructions and compiler optimizations based on community feedback.
